comment: COMP1511 is a fundamental introductory compulsory course for computer majors at UNSW, primarily teaching C language programming, basic algorithmic thinking, and standard methods for simple program design. The overall pace of the course is relatively tight (9 weeks + flex), but the content is arranged progressively from simple to more advanced (from the most basic C syntax to slightly complex data structures like structs and linked lists). It is suitable for students with little programming background to build a foundation, but those with absolutely no prior experience may feel some pressure in the mid-to-late stages of the semester. The strength of this course lies in its strong practical focus; labs, assignments, and autotests help students quickly develop the mindset of "writing code—debugging—improving." Although the content is introductory, it places significant demands on programming standards, logical expression, and problem decomposition skills, so the improvement after completing the course is quite noticeable. It also cultivates a habit of writing comments, laying the groundwork for subsequent courses, group collaboration, and code maintenance. The difficulty lies in the fact that the concepts may seem few early on, but once students delve into arrays, functions, pointers, structs, linked lists, and more complex program design, many begin to struggle. If students only attend lectures without practicing coding themselves, it’s easy to fall behind later. The importance of regular lab exercises becomes evident here. Additionally, assignments provide students with an opportunity to complete a small project over a longer period (2–3 weeks), accounting for about 30%–40% of the course grade. The assignment guide breaks down the entire project into smaller parts, guiding students to progressively complete the main portion of the project (usually around 80%; the remaining parts may involve content from later courses and are intended for students with some programming ability or those aiming for grades of 75+ or 85+). Students can choose to complete assignment content selectively based on their own abilities and the grade distribution. Finally, the exam typically accounts for 40%–50% of the course grade and consists of around 10 programming questions covering almost all data structures and functions learned throughout the semester. Students are generally required to complete at least 40% of the exam content (hurdle, which may include specified questions). One question might test a single data structure, while subsequent questions may involve the application of two or more data structures within a single problem. The last one or two questions may involve content from later courses and are intended for students with some programming ability or those aiming for grades of 75+ or 85+. Overall, COMP1511 is a highly foundational and valuable training course. It not only teaches C language syntax but, more importantly, helps students develop the fundamental mindset of computer science. This course is crucial for subsequent studies in data structures, algorithms, and systems-related courses.

COMP4920 is a course focused on professional ethics and technical ethics, with an emphasis not on programming implementation but on discussing ethical judgments, sense of responsibility, and the social impacts of technology applications in the computer science field. This course covers ethical theories, moral judgments, and the application of these frameworks to real-world computer science case analyses. The course is characterized by its strong emphasis on critical thinking and high demands for writing and argumentation, making it more suitable for students who have already taken multiple technical courses and wish to move beyond "how to build systems" to consider "why we do it this way and whether it is responsible." Its value lies not in improving coding skills but in helping students develop a more comprehensive professional perspective.

Overall, COMP4920 is more like a course that helps computer science students fill gaps in professional ethics and critical thinking. For students aiming to enter the software, AI, or broader technology industries, it encourages a shift from focusing solely on technical implementation to considering the responsibilities and impacts behind technical decisions.

Now, moving from the technical summary to some personal feelings: This course primarily covers computer ethics and morality. It doesn’t require any coding, but students have to write two essays and deliver a final presentation. Students need to choose a topic and read academic materials provided by the instructor or find relevant online sources to support their arguments. The process is extremely painful and torturous for students who aren’t particularly interested in this area. If the tutor is from a non-computer science background (e.g., philosophy), it can be even more torturous. Non-computer science tutors might provide "less accurate" guidance or assistance when it comes to topics or questions outside their expertise (such as specialized computer science knowledge), and they may grill your essay from their own professional perspective and way of thinking, which is especially torturous for students who haven’t systematically trained in logical reasoning. Additionally, the grading is very stingy and subjective. Basically, if the tutor is good, your grade won’t be too bad, but if the tutor is bad, you’re basically screwed.

The course arrangement for COMP2521 is meticulously designed, with specific themes and learning objectives each week. The course employs various formats such as lectures, videos, lab exercises, quizzes, and assignments to help students comprehensively grasp the knowledge of data structures and algorithms.  
Week 1: Introduction and Recursion  
Theme: Course introduction, recursion concepts, algorithm analysis.  
Resources: Video lectures, YouTube videos, code examples.  
Week 2: Sorting Algorithms  
Theme: Introduction to sorting algorithms, basic sorting, divide-and-conquer sorting, non-comparison sorting.  
Resources: Multiple video lectures, YouTube videos, code, and visualization tools.  
Week 3: Abstract Data Types  
Theme: Binary Search Trees.  
Resources: Video lectures, YouTube videos, code, and visualization tools.  
Week 4: Balanced Binary Trees  
Theme: Balanced binary trees, AVL trees.  
Resources: Video lectures, YouTube videos, code, and visualization tools.  
Week 5: Graph Basics and Traversal  
Theme: Basic concepts of graphs, graph traversal algorithms.  
Resources: Video lectures, YouTube videos, code, and visualization tools.  
Week 6: Flexible Learning Week  
Provides additional time for students to review and delve deeper into the material.  
Week 7: Directed Graph Algorithms  
Theme: Dijkstra's algorithm, minimum spanning trees.  
Resources: Video lectures, YouTube videos, code, and visualization tools.  
Week 8: Hash Tables  
Theme: Hash tables, applications of hash tables.  
Resources: Video lectures, YouTube videos, code, and visualization tools.  
Week 9: Priority Queues, Heaps, and Tries  
Theme: Priority queues, heaps, Trie trees.  
Resources: Video lectures, YouTube videos, code, and visualization tools.  
Week 10: Course Review and Exam  
Review the entire semester's content to prepare for the final exam.  
🎯 Learning Outcomes  
Through studying COMP2521, you will be able to:  
Analyze and measure algorithm performance.  
Select and develop appropriate data structures and algorithms for problems.  
Reason about the effectiveness of data structures and algorithms.  
Package data structures and algorithms as abstract data types.  
Develop complex software systems using the C language.

The good part is the high degree of freedom—you can choose your own direction, and if you’re genuinely interested in networking, you can actually learn a lot. But the problems are also pretty obvious: first, the barrier to entry is really high, with a bunch of prerequisites; without planning ahead, it’s basically impossible to get in. Second, spots are very limited—in my year, it was basically a scramble; if you were even slightly late, they were gone. Lastly, progress relies entirely on self-discipline; no one is constantly checking on you, so if you’re not self-motivated, it’s really easy to procrastinate until everything falls apart. Overall, it doesn’t feel like “taking a course” at all—more like being thrown into doing a mini research project on your own. If you’re just looking to breeze through for credits, it’ll really be a pain.

Also, 9992 requires a sufficient grade in 9991 (I think 75+) to continue, which directly filters out a bunch of people. 9993 feels more like wrapping things up—you do evaluation, comparison, final presentations, that kind of thing. If you’re already set on going into research or planning to apply for a Ph.D., this track can be quite useful.
